title: Guarantee genuine human review and disclosure before an algorithm penalises or deactivates a platform worker
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on two independent EU court rulings against algorithmic management of platform workers: Uber's Amsterdam 'robo-firing' case and Deliveroo's Bologna ranking-algorithm case. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the Phase 3 canonical expansion.

decision_statement: Before an algorithm restricts, suspends, or deactivates a platform worker's account, or otherwise materially affects their working conditions, the worker must be told the automated system's basis for the decision and given a genuine, human-reviewed opportunity to contest it — and any ranking or scoring logic must distinguish legally protected absences from unjustified ones.
decision_context: Motivated by two independent EU rulings within the same governance concept: Uber's Amsterdam court finding that 'robo-firing' with only symbolic human review violated GDPR Article 22, and Deliveroo's Bologna court finding that treating all rider absences identically was discriminatory.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Platform Worker Algorithmic Management Board
alternatives_considered: Treat algorithmic account deactivation as a routine automated business process not requiring worker-facing explanation.
Provide a generic appeals process without disclosing the automated system's specific basis for the decision.

citations.title: Rb. Amsterdam, 14 April 2021 — C/13/696010 / HA ZA 21-81
Sentenza Tribunale di Bologna, R.G. 2949/2019 (Sezione Lavoro)

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this ruling.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.
Worker-facing disclosure and human review directly satisfy the EU Platform Work Directive's algorithmic-management safeguards.
Compliance must be demonstrated by an observable worker appeal log.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether workers can actually obtain human review before losing income.
